description: We’re four students with a mix of skills. Data and ML (Python, pandas, statistics), backend development and UI, and web and game development. Between us we can take raw satellite data all the way to an interactive app people can actually use. We’re into Earth science, data visualization and building tools that solve real problems.
summary:
Since 2000, NASA satellites have recorded fire hotspots, but the counts from different satellites don’t line up. VIIRS (375 m pixels, from 2012) picks up many small fires that MODIS (about 1 km, from 2000) misses, and satellites keep being added and retired. So a raw fire count jumps in 2012, 2018 and 2023 even when nothing changed on the ground.
We built one fire record from 2000 to today that doesn’t jump. We grid NASA FIRMS hotspots at 0.25° per month, average per satellite, and convert MODIS counts to the VIIRS scale with a ratio fitted for each 2.5° zone and month of the year. To check it, we left 2020 out of the fit and predicted it: monthly error across India was 11.4%, compared with 24.8% for a single ratio.
Our web app covers India, Brazil, Australia, California and Greece. Pick a region or draw an area to see its fire calendar, live hotspots, and how this season compares with the last 26 years. In Punjab and Haryana, 1–13 November 2026 had 2,913 hotspots. The same days usually have about 24,037.
details:
Live app: https://prometheus-375.vercel.app

Code (MIT): https://github.com/karthik762/prometheus-375

What it does

Prometheus 375 puts MODIS and VIIRS fire detections on one scale, so you can compare any month from November 2000 to November 2026. Pick a preset region or draw an area, and it tells you whether this fire season is normal for that place.

How it works

1. We keep vegetation fires only and drop low-confidence detections (MODIS confidence below 30, VIIRS "low"). Near-real-time data has no fire-type field, so we mask known static heat sources such as factories. On held-out 2025 data for Punjab and Haryana, 0.30% of what was left were false positives.

2. We grid detections into 0.25° cells, by month and by satellite.

3. We average the satellites in each family instead of adding them up. That's why Aqua joining in 2002, NOAA-20 in 2018, NOAA-21 in 2023 and S-NPP stopping on 2 Nov 2026 don't show up as jumps.

4. We convert MODIS to the VIIRS scale with one ratio per 2.5° zone and month of the year. Punjab and Haryana get their own zone. Converted values carry an 80% uncertainty band from bootstrapping.

5. We compare each month with the same month in the 26 years before it (median, percentile, z-score) and estimate when the burning season started. November 2026 only has data up to the 13th, so we compare it with 1–13 November of earlier years instead of scaling it up.

Does it work?

We left 2020 out of the fit and predicted it. Monthly error, ours vs a single ratio: India 11.4% vs 24.8%, Punjab and Haryana 20.8% vs 75.6%, Brazil 7.9% vs 19.7%, Australia 9.4% vs 13.3%, California 15.6% vs 30.8%. Greece is where we lose, 26.6% vs 24.4%; it has too few fires for zone ratios to help. In Punjab's main burning months the error was small (October −1.5%, November +6.2%). Most of its 20.8% comes from months with almost no fires.

What we found

Burning in Punjab and Haryana has dropped sharply this year. 1–13 November 2026 had 2,913 hotspots against about 24,037 for the same days in a usual year. October had 1,517 against 31,634, the lowest in the record. The season hasn't really started, at least 28 days later than usual. We checked raw NOAA-20 counts to rule out missing data. One result surprised us: the MODIS-to-VIIRS ratio is lower in Punjab's peak burning months (8.35 in October, 9.52 in November) than for India overall (11.39). We expected the opposite.

The app

Region presets or a drawn area, a fire calendar from 2001 with MODIS-estimated years hatched, a before/after chart where the 2012 jump disappears, a now-vs-normal card, live NOAA-20/21 hotspots from the last 7 days, and CSV and PNG downloads. Areas outside our five regions say "no data" instead of showing zero.

Who it's for

Air-quality, farming and fire researchers need records that go back decades, and right now a change of satellite can look like a trend. Our record keeps going when satellites are added or retired.

What we thought about

Honesty about uncertainty mattered most to us. Pre-2012 values are estimates, so they're hatched and carry a band. We report where the method fails (Greece) instead of hiding it. Partial months are compared fairly, missing data never shows as zero, and the app refuses months that don't have data yet.

Built with

Python and DuckDB for the pipeline, FastAPI on Render for the API, React, TypeScript and MapLibre on Vercel for the app. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m).

Limits

Fires MODIS never saw can't be recovered. Results hold for regions and months, not single 0.25° cells. Clouds hide fires from every satellite.
